11	- `packages/adapter-*` - reserved for optional external-service adapters with their own dependency (`adapter-codex`, `adapter-jev`). New packages only at real boundaries: a different runtime, reuse by several apps, or an optional or licence-sensitive dependency (ADR-0014). Otherwise add a folder.
12	- `apps/*` - composition roots: `api`, `mcp`, `web`, `plugin-codex`, `plugin-claude`.
13	- `tooling/` - shared config and the repository gate scripts.
14	
15	Layer rules are enforced by `pnpm check:layers` (declared workspace dependencies) and `pnpm check:deps` (dependency-cruiser). Reach other packages only through their `@graphgoblin/*` entry points.
16	
17	Node 22 LTS is the supported runtime; installation, development and gates need Node 22.22.2 or later, and other majors are unsupported. Select it for the whole shell before running commands. On this Windows host that is the project-scoped runtime, leaving the machine's own Node untouched: `$env:PATH = "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude\codex-runs\GraphGoblin\runtime\node-v22.23.4-win-x64;$env:PATH"` in PowerShell, or `export PATH="$HOME/.claude/codex-runs/GraphGoblin/runtime/node-v22.23.4-win-x64:$PATH"` in Git Bash. Confirm `node --version` reports `v22.22.2` or later. `.nvmrc`, CI and the container use major 22 (CI and the container take the latest 22.x); root `engines.node` and `devEngines.runtime` declare `^22.22.2`, with `onFail: error` refusing every pnpm command on an older Node 22 or another major. pnpm runs package scripts with the first `node` on PATH. Run gates through pnpm: calling `node_modules/.bin/turbo` directly bypasses this check, and Turbo's cache key ignores the running Node version. See ADR-0040 and ADR-0058.
18	
19	## Rules
20	
21	- `tooling` participates in the shared Vitest V8 coverage gate and the Turbo lint pipeline; its independent built-app acceptance suites remain separate.
22	- Every package must keep unit-test coverage at or above 90% of lines and branches. `pnpm test:coverage` fails otherwise. Do not lower thresholds or add exclusions beyond generated code.
23	- `pnpm typecheck` runs `tsc -b tsconfig.build.json && tsc -p tsconfig.json` in every TypeScript package (the web app runs `tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit`), so test files and fixtures are type-checked too; fix their types rather than casting to `any`. `tooling` is JavaScript: it has lint and coverage, not a typecheck task.
24	- Tests, lint, and typechecking need no prior build in the TypeScript packages: each lists a `development` export condition pointing at its TypeScript source, which TypeScript, Vitest, and ESLint resolve. Node at runtime loads `dist/`, so run `pnpm build` before starting an app. A new TypeScript workspace package must follow the same export-map shape. `tooling` tests drive the built API and web app: Turbo builds them first, and a direct package test needs `pnpm build` first.
25	- API subprocess tests build the API first through Turbo's `test` and `test:coverage` task dependencies.
26	- Only permissive licences (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, ISC). `pnpm check:licenses` enforces the allowlist in `tooling/license-allowlist.json`; add a line to `docs/research/licenses.md` for every new dependency.
27	- Relative imports use explicit `.js` extensions (NodeNext). Zod 4: use `.prefault({})` for object defaults whose fields have defaults.
28	- Keep docs in sync: a behaviour change updates the relevant numbered doc; a decision change adds an ADR.
29	- Clean design over backward compatibility, until the owner says otherwise (2026-10-04): the product is not released and has no production users. Do not build compatibility schemas, deprecated input paths, tolerant parsing of old data shapes, or dual code paths. Change the contract to its clean shape. A schema change within the current format is an ordinary Drizzle migration that keeps existing data; Drizzle migrations are for schema changes only. Stored content that a change makes invalid is never rewritten by migration code: the CHANGELOG upgrade note says which stored values to correct and how (for example the SQL), and the orchestrator corrects the owner's store by hand (ADR-0062). A change of the stored, export or device-draft format moves the current format and refuses older data clearly, with no converter, and the owner resets with `--reset` (ADR-0042); say so, and what exports or clients must change, in the CHANGELOG upgrade notes.
30	- Before picking up a GitHub issue, read `docs/15-issue-workflow.md` for its gate, routing, and delivery rules.
31	- Commits carry no assistant attribution of any kind.
32	
33	## Commands
34	
35	On Windows PowerShell, call `pnpm.cmd` (the default execution policy blocks `pnpm.ps1`); Git Bash and cmd can use `pnpm` directly.
36	
37	```
38	pnpm install
39	pnpm build
40	pnpm test:coverage
41	pnpm lint
42	pnpm docs:generate  # regenerate docs/reference after a node schema or route change
43	pnpm check          # typecheck, lint, layers, deps, coverage, licences, generated docs
44	```

# Working in this repository

GraphGoblin is a pnpm + Turborepo monorepo in TypeScript. Read `docs/README.md` first; `docs/12-implementation-plan.md` says what is being built now and `docs/decisions/` records settled decisions.

## Layout

- `packages/contracts` - Zod schemas and types. Depends on zod only.
- `packages/domain` - pure logic over the contracts. No I/O.
- `packages/engine` - executor, run manager, node handlers, written against ports. `@graphgoblin/engine/testing` has fakes for every port.
- `packages/infrastructure` - Node implementations of the engine ports, one folder per concern (`src/sqlite`, `src/fs`, `src/process`, `src/http`, `src/scheduler`), each with its own `index.ts` and an `@graphgoblin/infrastructure/<folder>` subpath. Folders may import each other.
- `packages/adapter-*` - reserved for optional external-service adapters with their own dependency (`adapter-codex`, `adapter-jev`). New packages only at real boundaries: a different runtime, reuse by several apps, or an optional or licence-sensitive dependency (ADR-0014). Otherwise add a folder.
- `apps/*` - composition roots: `api`, `mcp`, `web`, `plugin-codex`, `plugin-claude`.
- `tooling/` - shared config and the repository gate scripts.

Layer rules are enforced by `pnpm check:layers` (declared workspace dependencies) and `pnpm check:deps` (dependency-cruiser). Reach other packages only through their `@graphgoblin/*` entry points.

Node 22 LTS is the supported runtime; installation, development and gates need Node 22.22.2 or later, and other majors are unsupported. Select it for the whole shell before running commands. On this Windows host that is the project-scoped runtime, leaving the machine's own Node untouched: `$env:PATH = "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude\codex-runs\GraphGoblin\runtime\node-v22.23.4-win-x64;$env:PATH"` in PowerShell, or `export PATH="$HOME/.claude/codex-runs/GraphGoblin/runtime/node-v22.23.4-win-x64:$PATH"` in Git Bash. Confirm `node --version` reports `v22.22.2` or later. `.nvmrc`, CI and the container use major 22 (CI and the container take the latest 22.x); root `engines.node` and `devEngines.runtime` declare `^22.22.2`, with `onFail: error` refusing every pnpm command on an older Node 22 or another major. pnpm runs package scripts with the first `node` on PATH. Run gates through pnpm: calling `node_modules/.bin/turbo` directly bypasses this check, and Turbo's cache key ignores the running Node version. See ADR-0040 and ADR-0058.

## Rules

- `tooling` participates in the shared Vitest V8 coverage gate and the Turbo lint pipeline; its independent built-app acceptance suites remain separate.
- Every package must keep unit-test coverage at or above 90% of lines and branches. `pnpm test:coverage` fails otherwise. Do not lower thresholds or add exclusions beyond generated code.
- `pnpm typecheck` runs `tsc -b tsconfig.build.json && tsc -p tsconfig.json` in every TypeScript package (the web app runs `tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit`), so test files and fixtures are type-checked too; fix their types rather than casting to `any`. `tooling` is JavaScript: it has lint and coverage, not a typecheck task.
- Tests, lint, and typechecking need no prior build in the TypeScript packages: each lists a `development` export condition pointing at its TypeScript source, which TypeScript, Vitest, and ESLint resolve. Node at runtime loads `dist/`, so run `pnpm build` before starting an app. A new TypeScript workspace package must follow the same export-map shape. `tooling` tests drive the built API and web app: Turbo builds them first, and a direct package test needs `pnpm build` first.
- API subprocess tests build the API first through Turbo's `test` and `test:coverage` task dependencies.
- Only permissive licences (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, ISC). `pnpm check:licenses` enforces the allowlist in `tooling/license-allowlist.json`; add a line to `docs/research/licenses.md` for every new dependency.
- Relative imports use explicit `.js` extensions (NodeNext). Zod 4: use `.prefault({})` for object defaults whose fields have defaults.
- Keep docs in sync: a behaviour change updates the relevant numbered doc; a decision change adds an ADR.
- Clean design over backward compatibility, until the owner says otherwise (2026-10-04): the product is not released and has no production users. Do not build compatibility schemas, deprecated input paths, tolerant parsing of old data shapes, or dual code paths. Change the contract to its clean shape. A schema change within the current format is an ordinary Drizzle migration that keeps existing data; Drizzle migrations are for schema changes only. Stored content that a change makes invalid is never rewritten by migration code: the CHANGELOG upgrade note says which stored values to correct and how (for example the SQL), and the orchestrator corrects the owner's store by hand (ADR-0062). A change of the stored, export or device-draft format moves the current format and refuses older data clearly, with no converter, and the owner resets with `--reset` (ADR-0042); say so, and what exports or clients must change, in the CHANGELOG upgrade notes.
- Before picking up a GitHub issue, read `docs/15-issue-workflow.md` for its gate, routing, and delivery rules.
- Commits carry no assistant attribution of any kind.

## Commands

On Windows PowerShell, call `pnpm.cmd` (the default execution policy blocks `pnpm.ps1`); Git Bash and cmd can use `pnpm` directly.

```
pnpm install
pnpm build
pnpm test:coverage
pnpm lint
pnpm docs:generate  # regenerate docs/reference after a node schema or route change
pnpm check          # typecheck, lint, layers, deps, coverage, licences, generated docs
```

1	# Review Policy
2	
3	Use this policy to keep automated review decision-relevant, auditable, and bounded.
4	
5	## Contents
6	
7	- The optimization target and change contract
8	- Finding admission and severity calibration
9	- Root-cause ledger and review-pass budget
10	- Scope-growth circuit breaker and follow-up issues
11	- Review failure modes, stacked PRs, and metrics
12	
13	## The Optimization Target
14	
15	Maximize useful root causes found per review pass, not comments produced. Give correctness, security, maintainability, testability, architecture boundaries, and code quality equal investigative attention. A finding is useful when it changes a merge decision, produces an in-scope fix, or creates a durable and correctly scoped follow-up. A finding is waste when it repeats settled feedback, reviews the wrong patch, converts preferences into blockers, fragments one root cause into many comments, or makes the current change absorb unrelated debt.
16	
17	## Required Change Contract
18	
19	Before implementation or review, make these fields visible:
20	
21	| Field | Purpose |
22	| --- | --- |
23	| Outcome | Defines what success changes for a user or system. |
24	| Acceptance evidence | Defines observable proof of completion. |
25	| Non-goals | Protects the change from adjacent design work. |
26	| Invariants | Names safety, compatibility, authority, or data properties that must hold. |
27	| Changed systems | Bounds the intended impact surface. |
28	| Known debt | Prevents rediscovery from becoming an accidental blocker. |
29	| Verification | Names the executable repository commands and CI gates that precede model review, including any known non-repeatable checks. |
30	| Authority | Records who may commit, publish, create tickets, expand scope, or merge. |
31	
32	## Finding Admission Tests
33	
34	Admit a root cause into the review only when every answer is yes:
35	
36	1. Is the evidence based on the current head and intended comparison base?
37	2. Does concrete code or behavior support the observation?
38	3. Is there a credible impact on runtime behavior, security, delivery, maintainability, testability, comprehensibility, architecture boundaries, or future change safety?
39	4. Can the reviewer state an actionable outcome without requiring one arbitrary implementation?
40	5. Is it not already fixed, represented by an existing issue, deferred with a durable link, rejected with evidence, inherited from the stack, stale, or represented by the same root cause?
41	
42	Admit a finding as a current-PR blocker only when the patch introduced or materially worsened it, a reachable failure threatens an accepted invariant or delivery gate, and resolving it belongs inside the change contract.
43	
44	Default other concrete findings to issue-ready P2 or P3 follow-ups. Reject purely aesthetic preferences, unsupported speculation, and observations without a meaningful maintenance or delivery cost.
45	
46	## Severity Calibration
47	
48	Severity describes urgency and merge impact, not the importance of the review domain. Maintainability and code quality deserve the same review attention as security while often producing a different disposition.
49	
50	- `P0`: active catastrophic exposure or corruption requiring an immediate stop.
51	- `P1`: reachable introduced security, authorization, data-loss, wrong-actuation, concurrency, recovery, build, or primary-path failure that should block merge.
52	- `P2`: important but non-catastrophic correctness, reliability, operability, maintainability, testability, architecture, or code-quality problem with concrete impact. It may be introduced or pre-existing. Default it to a follow-up issue unless the contract makes it in-scope or it must be fixed to merge safely.
53	- `P3`: localized, concrete improvement to clarity, cohesion, coupling, duplication, complexity, naming accuracy, documentation fidelity, tests, consistency, or future change safety. It is non-blocking and defaults to a follow-up issue.
54	
55	Repository-specific rules may make a deterministic policy violation actionable, but they do not automatically make it `P1`. Pre-existing debt does not become introduced merely because the changed code passes near it.
56	
57	## Root-Cause Ledger
58	
59	Track findings by stable root-cause signature rather than comment count:
60	
61	| Field | Example |
62	| --- | --- |
63	| Signature | `provider-dispatch/unknown-id-falls-back` |
64	| First seen | review request and head SHA |
65	| Evidence | affected path, behavior, and reproduction |
66	| Disposition | one of the four standard dispositions |
67	| Resolution | fix reference, issue link, or rejection reason |
68	| Verification | command, test, or inspection result |
69	
70	Do not request a reviewer to decide whether its own prior finding was in scope. The implementation agent applies the change contract and records the disposition.
71	
72	## Review-Pass Budget
73	
74	Use these defaults unless repository guidance sets a stricter budget:
75	
76	1. Stable full review after the configured repository gates.
77	2. Targeted re-review of the batched fix delta.
78	3. Exceptional targeted pass only when the fix introduced a credible `P0` or `P1`.
79	4. Any additional pass requires human authorization and a written reason.
80	
81	If the head changed only by rebase or restack, compare patch identity before reviewing. Skip review when the effective patch is unchanged.
82	
83	## Scope-Growth Circuit Breaker
84	
85	Pause for human direction when any of these occurs:
86	
87	- a proposed fix adds a new subsystem or architectural layer;
88	- the changed-file set or behavioral surface grows materially beyond the contract;
89	- a finding requires selecting among product or architecture alternatives;
90	- the same root cause returns after an evidenced resolution;
91	- the reviewer requires implementation of explicitly linked deferred work;
92	- review comments outnumber distinct root causes by a large margin;
93	- a pass is clean and another pass is requested without a changed patch.
94	
95	The appropriate response is often a linked follow-up issue, not a larger pull request.
96	
97	## Follow-Up Issue Quality
98	
99	A durable follow-up issue should contain:
100	
101	- a duplicate check against open and recently closed issues;
102	- origin PR and relevant review link;
103	- one root cause, not a transcript dump;
104	- current behavior and material impact;
105	- why it is outside the current contract;
106	- acceptance criteria;
107	- known constraints and verification expectations.
108	
109	A local TODO is optional. Use it only at a concrete code seam and link the issue. Do not let a TODO silently become a second specification or a reviewer-enforced blocker.
110	
111	The reviewer should identify a follow-up candidate, not order or perform the external write. The parent development pipeline decides the disposition, checks authority, deduplicates, creates the issue when authorized, and links the result back to the originating thread.
112	
113	Default every admitted P2 and P3 finding to an issue-ready follow-up unless an existing issue already represents the root cause. This default does not authorize issue spam: group symptoms, reject aesthetic-only preferences, and reuse existing issues.
114	
115	## Review Failure Modes
116	
117	Guard explicitly against:
118	
119	- **Scope inflation:** do not require P2 or P3 work in the current PR merely because it is valuable.
120	- **Severity inflation:** do not label maintainability feedback P1 just to force visibility.
121	- **Quality blindness:** do not ignore maintainability, tests, boundaries, coupling, complexity, duplication, or documentation fidelity merely because they are non-blocking.
122	- **Stale repetition:** do not re-raise fixed, rejected, issue-linked, inherited, or old-head findings without new contradictory evidence.
123	- **Wrong-base review:** do not review a stacked child against the repository default branch.
124	- **Symptom fragmentation:** produce one finding and one follow-up issue per root cause.
125	- **Design over-prescription:** state the violated invariant and required outcome rather than demanding one architecture.
126	- **Speculative noise:** require a concrete maintenance, comprehension, testability, or delivery cost rather than taste alone.
127	- **Mechanical-review churn:** rely on executable repository gates for formatting and lint; when a recurring mechanical problem reveals a missing gate, propose one P3 follow-up for the enforcement gap.
128	- **Clean-review resistance:** do not manufacture a new observation when the current patch has no new root cause.
129	
130	## Stacked Pull Requests
131	
132	- Record the immediate parent for each child.
133	- Review the child relative to that parent, not the repository default branch.
134	- Do not file inherited parent findings against every child.
135	- Re-review after restacking only when patch identity or conflict resolution changed behavior.
136	- Keep one root-cause ledger per effective patch so duplicate findings across the stack can be recognized.
137	
138	## Useful Process Metrics
139	
140	Measure trends by distinct root causes, not raw comments:
141	
142	- accepted introduced defects per full review;
143	- duplicate or stale finding rate;
144	- deferred issue completion rate;
145	- review passes per merged change;
146	- clean reviews with no intervening patch;
147	- scope growth after review begins;
148	- time from first stable review to terminal decision;
149	- reviewer tokens per accepted root cause;
150	- total review-and-repair tokens per terminal decision;
151	- reopened root causes after an evidenced disposition.
152	
153	Do not optimize for zero findings. Optimize for few repeated findings, high accepted-finding precision, durable deferred work, and bounded time to a merge decision.

# Review Policy

Use this policy to keep automated review decision-relevant, auditable, and bounded.

## Contents

- The optimization target and change contract
- Finding admission and severity calibration
- Root-cause ledger and review-pass budget
- Scope-growth circuit breaker and follow-up issues
- Review failure modes, stacked PRs, and metrics

## The Optimization Target

Maximize useful root causes found per review pass, not comments produced. Give correctness, security, maintainability, testability, architecture boundaries, and code quality equal investigative attention. A finding is useful when it changes a merge decision, produces an in-scope fix, or creates a durable and correctly scoped follow-up. A finding is waste when it repeats settled feedback, reviews the wrong patch, converts preferences into blockers, fragments one root cause into many comments, or makes the current change absorb unrelated debt.

## Required Change Contract

Before implementation or review, make these fields visible:

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Outcome | Defines what success changes for a user or system. |
| Acceptance evidence | Defines observable proof of completion. |
| Non-goals | Protects the change from adjacent design work. |
| Invariants | Names safety, compatibility, authority, or data properties that must hold. |
| Changed systems | Bounds the intended impact surface. |
| Known debt | Prevents rediscovery from becoming an accidental blocker. |
| Verification | Names the executable repository commands and CI gates that precede model review, including any known non-repeatable checks. |
| Authority | Records who may commit, publish, create tickets, expand scope, or merge. |

## Finding Admission Tests

Admit a root cause into the review only when every answer is yes:

1. Is the evidence based on the current head and intended comparison base?
2. Does concrete code or behavior support the observation?
3. Is there a credible impact on runtime behavior, security, delivery, maintainability, testability, comprehensibility, architecture boundaries, or future change safety?
4. Can the reviewer state an actionable outcome without requiring one arbitrary implementation?
5. Is it not already fixed, represented by an existing issue, deferred with a durable link, rejected with evidence, inherited from the stack, stale, or represented by the same root cause?

Admit a finding as a current-PR blocker only when the patch introduced or materially worsened it, a reachable failure threatens an accepted invariant or delivery gate, and resolving it belongs inside the change contract.

Default other concrete findings to issue-ready P2 or P3 follow-ups. Reject purely aesthetic preferences, unsupported speculation, and observations without a meaningful maintenance or delivery cost.

## Severity Calibration

Severity describes urgency and merge impact, not the importance of the review domain. Maintainability and code quality deserve the same review attention as security while often producing a different disposition.

- `P0`: active catastrophic exposure or corruption requiring an immediate stop.
- `P1`: reachable introduced security, authorization, data-loss, wrong-actuation, concurrency, recovery, build, or primary-path failure that should block merge.
- `P2`: important but non-catastrophic correctness, reliability, operability, maintainability, testability, architecture, or code-quality problem with concrete impact. It may be introduced or pre-existing. Default it to a follow-up issue unless the contract makes it in-scope or it must be fixed to merge safely.
- `P3`: localized, concrete improvement to clarity, cohesion, coupling, duplication, complexity, naming accuracy, documentation fidelity, tests, consistency, or future change safety. It is non-blocking and defaults to a follow-up issue.

Repository-specific rules may make a deterministic policy violation actionable, but they do not automatically make it `P1`. Pre-existing debt does not become introduced merely because the changed code passes near it.

## Root-Cause Ledger

Track findings by stable root-cause signature rather than comment count:

| Field | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Signature | `provider-dispatch/unknown-id-falls-back` |
| First seen | review request and head SHA |
| Evidence | affected path, behavior, and reproduction |
| Disposition | one of the four standard dispositions |
| Resolution | fix reference, issue link, or rejection reason |
| Verification | command, test, or inspection result |

Do not request a reviewer to decide whether its own prior finding was in scope. The implementation agent applies the change contract and records the disposition.

## Review-Pass Budget

Use these defaults unless repository guidance sets a stricter budget:

1. Stable full review after the configured repository gates.
2. Targeted re-review of the batched fix delta.
3. Exceptional targeted pass only when the fix introduced a credible `P0` or `P1`.
4. Any additional pass requires human authorization and a written reason.

If the head changed only by rebase or restack, compare patch identity before reviewing. Skip review when the effective patch is unchanged.

## Scope-Growth Circuit Breaker

Pause for human direction when any of these occurs:

- a proposed fix adds a new subsystem or architectural layer;
- the changed-file set or behavioral surface grows materially beyond the contract;
- a finding requires selecting among product or architecture alternatives;
- the same root cause returns after an evidenced resolution;
- the reviewer requires implementation of explicitly linked deferred work;
- review comments outnumber distinct root causes by a large margin;
- a pass is clean and another pass is requested without a changed patch.

The appropriate response is often a linked follow-up issue, not a larger pull request.

## Follow-Up Issue Quality

A durable follow-up issue should contain:

- a duplicate check against open and recently closed issues;
- origin PR and relevant review link;
- one root cause, not a transcript dump;
- current behavior and material impact;
- why it is outside the current contract;
- acceptance criteria;
- known constraints and verification expectations.

A local TODO is optional. Use it only at a concrete code seam and link the issue. Do not let a TODO silently become a second specification or a reviewer-enforced blocker.

The reviewer should identify a follow-up candidate, not order or perform the external write. The parent development pipeline decides the disposition, checks authority, deduplicates, creates the issue when authorized, and links the result back to the originating thread.

Default every admitted P2 and P3 finding to an issue-ready follow-up unless an existing issue already represents the root cause. This default does not authorize issue spam: group symptoms, reject aesthetic-only preferences, and reuse existing issues.

## Review Failure Modes

Guard explicitly against:

- **Scope inflation:** do not require P2 or P3 work in the current PR merely because it is valuable.
- **Severity inflation:** do not label maintainability feedback P1 just to force visibility.
- **Quality blindness:** do not ignore maintainability, tests, boundaries, coupling, complexity, duplication, or documentation fidelity merely because they are non-blocking.
- **Stale repetition:** do not re-raise fixed, rejected, issue-linked, inherited, or old-head findings without new contradictory evidence.
- **Wrong-base review:** do not review a stacked child against the repository default branch.
- **Symptom fragmentation:** produce one finding and one follow-up issue per root cause.
- **Design over-prescription:** state the violated invariant and required outcome rather than demanding one architecture.
- **Speculative noise:** require a concrete maintenance, comprehension, testability, or delivery cost rather than taste alone.
- **Mechanical-review churn:** rely on executable repository gates for formatting and lint; when a recurring mechanical problem reveals a missing gate, propose one P3 follow-up for the enforcement gap.
- **Clean-review resistance:** do not manufacture a new observation when the current patch has no new root cause.

## Stacked Pull Requests

- Record the immediate parent for each child.
- Review the child relative to that parent, not the repository default branch.
- Do not file inherited parent findings against every child.
- Re-review after restacking only when patch identity or conflict resolution changed behavior.
- Keep one root-cause ledger per effective patch so duplicate findings across the stack can be recognized.

## Useful Process Metrics

Measure trends by distinct root causes, not raw comments:

- accepted introduced defects per full review;
- duplicate or stale finding rate;
- deferred issue completion rate;
- review passes per merged change;
- clean reviews with no intervening patch;
- scope growth after review begins;
- time from first stable review to terminal decision;
- reviewer tokens per accepted root cause;
- total review-and-repair tokens per terminal decision;
- reopened root causes after an evidenced disposition.

Do not optimize for zero findings. Optimize for few repeated findings, high accepted-finding precision, durable deferred work, and bounded time to a merge decision.

After the merge a human exercises the merged build, records the commit or build, their observations and the outcome on the tracking item, and closes it. Human QA is tracked separately from implementation, review, agent QA, CI and merge, as one of: not required, pending merge, pending human QA, or completed with an evidence link. 45	| 4    | `gpt-6-astra`     | Hardest work and escalation |
46

51	Every issue has one type: `type:bug`, `type:feature`, `type:ui-polish`, `type:architecture`, `type:chore`, `type:research`, or `type:epic`. 52	
53	Milestones are `Pre-merge #151` for work that must land before the feature PR merges, `After merge: evaluate and stabilise` for product evaluation, the architecture sweep and the cutovers they require (this milestone blocks further feature work), and `Later` for queued and long-term work, with most items parked under `backlog`.

Every pull request for a `human-in-the-loop` issue carries a post-merge human QA checklist with expected observations and names an open tracking item (the issue itself or a linked QA item). 480	## Codex adapter for 1.0 (Decided)
481	
482	### Facts the design relies on
483	
484	Verified on 2026-10-02 against the `openai/codex` repository and docs. Full notes in `research/codex-sdk.md`.
485	
486	- `@openai/codex-sdk` is Apache-2.0 and requires Node 18 or newer. It is pinned exactly at 0.160.0. It depends on `@openai/codex` at the same version, which ships the native CLI, and by default runs that bundled binary (the adapter's `codexBinary` option overrides it). It exchanges JSONL events with the CLI over stdio.
487	- Threads persist under `~/.codex/sessions` and can be resumed with `resumeThread(id, options)`.
488	- `run` and `runStreamed` accept an `outputSchema` for structured output and an AbortSignal.
489	- `runStreamed` yields `thread.started`, `turn.started`, `item.started|updated|completed`, `turn.completed` (usage), `turn.failed`, and `error` events.
490	- The client accepts `codexPathOverride`, `env`, `baseUrl`, `apiKey`, `config` (flattened to dotted `--config` keys), and `configOverrides` (raw `key=value` strings). Thread options are `model`, `modelReasoningEffort`, `sandboxMode`, `approvalPolicy`, `networkAccessEnabled`, `webSearchMode`, `webSearchEnabled`, `workingDirectory`, `skipGitRepoCheck`, `additionalDirectories`, and `threadSource`.
491	- Reasoning effort values used are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max` (`model_reasoning_effort`), as the CLI's own model catalog lists them per model (see "Model catalog").
492	- Codex has a native Windows sandbox since March 2026, and plugins bundling skills, MCP servers, and connectors since CLI 0.117.0.
493	
494	All of this was verified against the pinned version in M4; `research/codex-sdk.md` lists every option with the CLI argument it becomes.
495	
496	### Authentication (Decided)
497	
498	GraphGoblin uses the machine's existing Codex login, which may be a ChatGPT subscription. It never stores or proxies Codex credentials. The adapter's `preflight` runs the CLI to confirm it is installed and authenticated, and the settings page shows the result. If an API key is desired later, it is passed through `env`, never persisted by GraphGoblin.
499	
500	### Mapping inference config to the SDK (Decided, verified in M4)
501	
502	An enabled GraphGoblin catalogue entry or a ready preflight does not establish that the selected
503	model is available to the API process user's actual Codex login and provider endpoint. Preflight
504	checks installation, supported CLI capabilities and authentication without requesting a model turn.
505	The bundled CLI's static model/plan metadata is not a live entitlement check. The October 2026
506	ChatGPT-account refusal for `gpt-5.5` in [#427](https://github.com/Jacob-J-Thomas/GraphGoblin/issues/427)
507	is dated evidence, not a universal current restriction or proof that an API key always fixes it.
508	
509	For a structured HTTP 400 `invalid_request_error`, the adapter keeps the provider's explanation
510	as `HARNESS_ARGUMENTS_REJECTED`; the run records `HARNESS_TURN_FAILED` with that adapter code and
511	does not offer Resume. An account/endpoint explanation is evidence for that refused request,
512	not a diagnosis for every unavailable model or unknown provider error. Deliberately choose a
513	model supported for that login/endpoint, or change the login/endpoint as the API process user;
514	correct the applicable definition/default and start a new run. GraphGoblin does not substitute
515	another model or globally disable a seed from one account's refusal. See
516	[model-access troubleshooting](guide/07-troubleshooting.md#codex-model-unavailable-for-this-account-or-endpoint).
517	
518	Every behaviour-affecting setting a node has is passed as a per-thread option on every session, so the machine's `config.toml` values for them (on the owner's machine: model `gpt-6.1-sol`, effort `xhigh`, sandbox `danger-full-access`, approval `never`) never apply to a loop. Thread options become CLI arguments that come after any `config` overrides, so they also win over `configOverrides`.
519	
520	Codex turns inherit the user's configured plugins, including their enabled/disabled state and plugin-provided tools/services ([ADR-0067](decisions/ADR-0067-codex-inherits-configured-plugins.md)). No default `features.plugins` override is injected. An inference node opts out of all plugins by adding `"features":{"plugins":false}` to its existing `harnessOptions.configOverrides`; this includes resumes and same-session output-schema repairs. An explicit `true` can override a user feature disable while respecting individually disabled plugins. Individual plugin IDs contain `@` and cannot pass the node override key validation.
521	
522	LLM decisions and `coerce`/output-transform repairs use separate structured calls with no node overrides. Their current callers supply no working directory, so those calls start in a fresh temporary directory and inherit user/global Codex configuration, not the caller's inference override or trusted-project layer. Disable the plugin feature or an individual plugin in effective user/global configuration to exclude it from those calls; this also changes ordinary Codex sessions. There is no per-node structured-call plugin opt-out.
523	
524	Other extension isolation remains ([ADR-0063](decisions/ADR-0063-loop-turns-without-personal-extensions.md)). Before each turn the adapter runs `codex mcp list --json` in the turn's working directory **with plugins switched off only for discovery**, so plugin-owned servers are not listed and then suppressed. It starts the turn with every listed standalone MCP server disabled (`mcp_servers.<name>.enabled=false`), with `features.apps`, `features.memories`, `features.hooks`, `features.multi_agent` (sub-agent spawning) and `features.goals` false, and with `notify=[]`. If the listing fails, the turn does not start. Plain `--config` overrides cannot clear a table such as `mcp_servers={}`, because the CLI merges them into the loaded configuration; standalone servers are therefore disabled by name and remain available through explicit node overrides.
525	
526	Configuration errors reported by the CLI retain their pre-submission refusal. Plugin inheritance follows normal CLI resolution, rather than checking package health: pinned CLI 0.160.0 silently skips unknown plugin IDs and missing plugin MCP files. A successful turn does not prove every configured plugin loaded; [#442](https://github.com/Jacob-J-Thomas/GraphGoblin/issues/442) tracks diagnostics for that limit.
527	
528	Every listed server name and every segment of a node's override key must be one plain TOML key (letters, digits, `_`, `-`), and not `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype`. The shared contract checks raw authored keys before record parsing, including dotted keys, nested tables and tables inside arrays. The editor and API reject an invalid key with its field path instead of discarding it; publication also checks retained drafts and reports `CODEX_CONFIG_KEY_INVALID` on the inference node. Ordinary scalar values, valid tables and dotted keys keep their existing behavior. A previously stored invalid-key draft remains unchanged when publication is refused. Such stored definitions must be corrected before restarting with this contract, because the existing store guard refuses invalid definitions (see the CHANGELOG upgrade note).
529	
530	A listed server name that breaks this rule refuses the turn with `HARNESS_TURN_FAILED` (resumable once the machine's configuration is fixed). The adapter independently checks overrides with the same key rule and refuses them with `HARNESS_INVALID_CONFIGURATION`. The run records this as a non-resumable `HARNESS_TURN_FAILED` with that adapter code, so the node must change. Both are definitely not submitted. Existing HTTP reserved-key guards continue to apply before contract validation.
531	
532	API request-schema paths preserve literal authored member names with RFC 6901 escaping, including
533	`/` and `~` and nested array positions ([API error responses](07-api-and-streaming.md#error-responses-decided)).
534	Recovery of a manually edited stored row needs more than removing its bad override key: if its
535	defaulted harness was omitted, explicitly store `harness: "codex"` in the node configuration as
536	part of the operator correction on the stopped target store, alongside the key repair. Normal
537	API writes already materialize that value. Startup and input-schema validation do not rewrite a
538	stored omission; key-only repair can allow startup while GET and publication still fail. The
539	CHANGELOG recipe identifies the target and full backup procedure, limits any copy rehearsal to
540	offline checks without a gateway, and requires both discovery queries plus exact stored-text
541	readback because SQLite's affected-row count alone does not prove a quoted member changed. Before

## Codex adapter for 1.0 (Decided)

### Facts the design relies on

Verified on 2026-10-02 against the `openai/codex` repository and docs. Full notes in `research/codex-sdk.md`.

- `@openai/codex-sdk` is Apache-2.0 and requires Node 18 or newer. It is pinned exactly at 0.160.0. It depends on `@openai/codex` at the same version, which ships the native CLI, and by default runs that bundled binary (the adapter's `codexBinary` option overrides it). It exchanges JSONL events with the CLI over stdio.
- Threads persist under `~/.codex/sessions` and can be resumed with `resumeThread(id, options)`.
- `run` and `runStreamed` accept an `outputSchema` for structured output and an AbortSignal.
- `runStreamed` yields `thread.started`, `turn.started`, `item.started|updated|completed`, `turn.completed` (usage), `turn.failed`, and `error` events.
- The client accepts `codexPathOverride`, `env`, `baseUrl`, `apiKey`, `config` (flattened to dotted `--config` keys), and `configOverrides` (raw `key=value` strings). Thread options are `model`, `modelReasoningEffort`, `sandboxMode`, `approvalPolicy`, `networkAccessEnabled`, `webSearchMode`, `webSearchEnabled`, `workingDirectory`, `skipGitRepoCheck`, `additionalDirectories`, and `threadSource`.
- Reasoning effort values used are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max` (`model_reasoning_effort`), as the CLI's own model catalog lists them per model (see "Model catalog").
- Codex has a native Windows sandbox since March 2026, and plugins bundling skills, MCP servers, and connectors since CLI 0.117.0.

All of this was verified against the pinned version in M4; `research/codex-sdk.md` lists every option with the CLI argument it becomes.

### Authentication (Decided)

GraphGoblin uses the machine's existing Codex login, which may be a ChatGPT subscription. It never stores or proxies Codex credentials. The adapter's `preflight` runs the CLI to confirm it is installed and authenticated, and the settings page shows the result. If an API key is desired later, it is passed through `env`, never persisted by GraphGoblin.

### Mapping inference config to the SDK (Decided, verified in M4)

An enabled GraphGoblin catalogue entry or a ready preflight does not establish that the selected
model is available to the API process user's actual Codex login and provider endpoint. Preflight
checks installation, supported CLI capabilities and authentication without requesting a model turn.
The bundled CLI's static model/plan metadata is not a live entitlement check. The October 2026
ChatGPT-account refusal for `gpt-5.5` in [#427](https://github.com/Jacob-J-Thomas/GraphGoblin/issues/427)
is dated evidence, not a universal current restriction or proof that an API key always fixes it.

For a structured HTTP 400 `invalid_request_error`, the adapter keeps the provider's explanation
as `HARNESS_ARGUMENTS_REJECTED`; the run records `HARNESS_TURN_FAILED` with that adapter code and
does not offer Resume. An account/endpoint explanation is evidence for that refused request,
not a diagnosis for every unavailable model or unknown provider error. Deliberately choose a
model supported for that login/endpoint, or change the login/endpoint as the API process user;
correct the applicable definition/default and start a new run. GraphGoblin does not substitute
another model or globally disable a seed from one account's refusal. See
[model-access troubleshooting](guide/07-troubleshooting.md#codex-model-unavailable-for-this-account-or-endpoint).

Every behaviour-affecting setting a node has is passed as a per-thread option on every session, so the machine's `config.toml` values for them (on the owner's machine: model `gpt-6.1-sol`, effort `xhigh`, sandbox `danger-full-access`, approval `never`) never apply to a loop. Thread options become CLI arguments that come after any `config` overrides, so they also win over `configOverrides`.

Codex turns inherit the user's configured plugins, including their enabled/disabled state and plugin-provided tools/services ([ADR-0067](decisions/ADR-0067-codex-inherits-configured-plugins.md)). No default `features.plugins` override is injected. An inference node opts out of all plugins by adding `"features":{"plugins":false}` to its existing `harnessOptions.configOverrides`; this includes resumes and same-session output-schema repairs. An explicit `true` can override a user feature disable while respecting individually disabled plugins. Individual plugin IDs contain `@` and cannot pass the node override key validation.

LLM decisions and `coerce`/output-transform repairs use separate structured calls with no node overrides. Their current callers supply no working directory, so those calls start in a fresh temporary directory and inherit user/global Codex configuration, not the caller's inference override or trusted-project layer. Disable the plugin feature or an individual plugin in effective user/global configuration to exclude it from those calls; this also changes ordinary Codex sessions. There is no per-node structured-call plugin opt-out.

Other extension isolation remains ([ADR-0063](decisions/ADR-0063-loop-turns-without-personal-extensions.md)). Before each turn the adapter runs `codex mcp list --json` in the turn's working directory **with plugins switched off only for discovery**, so plugin-owned servers are not listed and then suppressed. It starts the turn with every listed standalone MCP server disabled (`mcp_servers.<name>.enabled=false`), with `features.apps`, `features.memories`, `features.hooks`, `features.multi_agent` (sub-agent spawning) and `features.goals` false, and with `notify=[]`. If the listing fails, the turn does not start. Plain `--config` overrides cannot clear a table such as `mcp_servers={}`, because the CLI merges them into the loaded configuration; standalone servers are therefore disabled by name and remain available through explicit node overrides.

Configuration errors reported by the CLI retain their pre-submission refusal. Plugin inheritance follows normal CLI resolution, rather than checking package health: pinned CLI 0.160.0 silently skips unknown plugin IDs and missing plugin MCP files. A successful turn does not prove every configured plugin loaded; [#442](https://github.com/Jacob-J-Thomas/GraphGoblin/issues/442) tracks diagnostics for that limit.

Every listed server name and every segment of a node's override key must be one plain TOML key (letters, digits, `_`, `-`), and not `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype`. The shared contract checks raw authored keys before record parsing, including dotted keys, nested tables and tables inside arrays. The editor and API reject an invalid key with its field path instead of discarding it; publication also checks retained drafts and reports `CODEX_CONFIG_KEY_INVALID` on the inference node. Ordinary scalar values, valid tables and dotted keys keep their existing behavior. A previously stored invalid-key draft remains unchanged when publication is refused. Such stored definitions must be corrected before restarting with this contract, because the existing store guard refuses invalid definitions (see the CHANGELOG upgrade note).

A listed server name that breaks this rule refuses the turn with `HARNESS_TURN_FAILED` (resumable once the machine's configuration is fixed). The adapter independently checks overrides with the same key rule and refuses them with `HARNESS_INVALID_CONFIGURATION`. The run records this as a non-resumable `HARNESS_TURN_FAILED` with that adapter code, so the node must change. Both are definitely not submitted. Existing HTTP reserved-key guards continue to apply before contract validation.

API request-schema paths preserve literal authored member names with RFC 6901 escaping, including
`/` and `~` and nested array positions ([API error responses](07-api-and-streaming.md#error-responses-decided)).
Recovery of a manually edited stored row needs more than removing its bad override key: if its
defaulted harness was omitted, explicitly store `harness: "codex"` in the node configuration as
part of the operator correction on the stopped target store, alongside the key repair. Normal
API writes already materialize that value. Startup and input-schema validation do not rewrite a
stored omission; key-only repair can allow startup while GET and publication still fail. The
CHANGELOG recipe identifies the target and full backup procedure, limits any copy rehearsal to
offline checks without a gateway, and requires both discovery queries plus exact stored-text
readback because SQLite's affected-row count alone does not prove a quoted member changed. Before
restart, correct applicable editable rows, resolve invalid-key discovery results and choose a
deliberate disposition for any actually incompatible snapshots. An omitted harness alone in an
immutable snapshot is accepted by definition parsing. An explicit version read of that manually
authored snapshot can still return `500 RESPONSE_INVALID`. Preserve its history.
If recovery uses a fresh store, adopt that store's configuration and credentials and use the loop
ID returned by import. An incompatible snapshot still blocks the original database. After the
operator starts the chosen store for normal service, authenticated read-only GET verifies
its served draft/current definitions; offline checks cover other retained versions. Verification
does not publish owner drafts or start runs. Publication and restart tests use separate synthetic
fixtures with fake harnesses and timers disabled, not a copy of the owner's store. No runtime
converter or backfill is provided (ADR-0062).

A loop turn still inherits from the machine:

- the login, the model catalog and the account's model access;
- the CLI's Windows sandbox backend selection (`windows.sandbox`), unless an explicit node
  config override supplies it. The SDK's `sandboxMode`
  becomes the separate `--sandbox` permission level; it does not select that Windows backend.
  GraphGoblin supplies no dedicated backend selection. The inheritance alone
  is not evidence that the node's sandbox permissions were weakened;
- the CLI's other built-in features at their defaults. This includes the code-mode host (`codex-code-mode-host.exe`), which is the CLI's own tool host, not an extension: without it a turn runs no command;
- the rest of `config.toml` that no node setting covers, such as project trust, model providers, `service_tier`, `personality`, `shell_environment_policy`, the skills under `CODEX_HOME` and the personal `AGENTS.md`. These familiar defaults are accepted by the owner's D2 decision, rather than left unresolved.

| Inference config                               | SDK mechanism (`@openai/codex-sdk` 0.160.0)                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `model`                                        | thread option `model` (`--model`); default from the engine's model resolution, else the adapter's `model` option (`gpt-6-luna`)                                                                                                                                      |
| `effort`                                       | thread option `modelReasoningEffort` (`model_reasoning_effort`); every level is sent under its own name except `none`, which is sent under the model family's name for it (below); the catalog limits which a model offers                                           |
| `harnessOptions.sandbox`                       | thread option `sandboxMode` (`--sandbox`): `read-only`, `workspace-write`, `danger-full-access`                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `harnessOptions.approval`                      | thread option `approvalPolicy` (`approval_policy`): `never` or `on-request`                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `harnessOptions.networkAccess`                 | thread option `networkAccessEnabled` (`sandbox_workspace_write.network_access`), always set, default `false`                                                                                                                                                         |
| `harnessOptions.webSearch`                     | thread option `webSearchMode` (`web_search`): `live` when true, otherwise `disabled`                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `harnessOptions.configOverrides`               | client `config` (dotted `--config` keys), layered after the isolation defaults and before the thread options (ADR-0063); `mcp_servers.<name>.enabled = true` re-enables a machine server; values that are not TOML (null, non-finite numbers, functions) are dropped |
| `capabilities.mcpServers`, `plugins`, `skills` | Not yet resolved for Codex: the port receives slugs only and there is no capability profile store. Codex logs and ignores them; use Codex-only `configOverrides` (`mcp_servers.<name>.*`, as above) until profiles land. Claude rejects nonempty capability lists.   |

1	# WP-F5: Windows command-launch diagnosis
2	
3	Research record for #102 (WP-F5), measured on 2026-10-19 from `main` at `9070207`. All launches used installed CLIs through their subscription logins, disposable directories, and disposable APIs on ports 5710 and 5711. No model turn was run for either provider. No credential was exported or printed: the CLIs only checked their own logins, and Claude's `auth status` output was reduced to two fields. The disposable APIs seeded the machine's Jev key from the environment into their own stores, as any instance does; those stores were deleted afterwards. The owner's instance, store and checkout were not touched. Revised on 2026-10-20 after review: the `fs.mkdtemp` boundary was re-measured at 247 characters (succeeds) and 248 (fails), and the defect classification of launch names was corrected.
4	
5	## Result
6	
7	**Confirmed, not a GraphGoblin launch defect.** The #102 failure (`Failed to create unified exec process: CreateProcessWithLogonW failed: 267`) is Codex's Windows sandbox refusing a command whose working directory is invalid. In the trial, the QA worker model supplied a per-command `workdir` that dropped one segment of the admitted workspace path, so the directory did not exist. GraphGoblin's `--cd` was correct, and every command that used it ran. The failure reproduces without a model turn by asking Codex's sandbox to start a command in a missing directory.
8	
9	**One matrix cell failed where the direct invocation succeeded,** and it was fixed: with the system temporary directory at 226 characters, the Claude adapter's readiness check could not create its empty check directory, because Windows `fs.mkdtemp` refuses paths of 248 characters or more (the check path was 249). Claude itself starts from such a directory. The adapter now creates the directory with `mkdir`. Every other cell behaved the same through GraphGoblin as through PowerShell and `cmd`.
10	
11	**Script node launches** behaved identically to direct launches in every matrix cell. The original report concerns harness launches (commands run by a Codex worker inside Codex's sandbox), not script nodes.
12	
13	## Environment
14	
15	| Item                     | Value                                                                                                                                                       |
16	| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
17	| OS                       | Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26300, `LongPathsEnabled = 1`, console code page 65001                                                                                  |
18	| Node                     | 22.14.0 for every GraphGoblin launch and every `codex.js` cell; the machine default 23.10.0 ran the npm global `codex.cmd` shim and read Codex session logs |
19	| Codex CLI                | 0.160.0, both the SDK-bundled CLI and the npm global install; the user Codex configuration selects `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"`                         |
20	| Claude Code              | 2.1.304, native `claude.exe`, signed in with a Claude.ai account                                                                                            |
21	| Other drive              | `D:` (local NTFS)                                                                                                                                           |
22	| Session variables        | The Claude Code session variables of the measuring shell (`CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_CODE_*`, `CLAUDE_PID`) were removed from every launched environment         |
23	| Updater on Claude copies | Direct launches of copied `claude.exe` set `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1`, as the product's own Claude environment does                                            |
24	
25	## The original report
26	
27	The 2026-10-06 trial ran one QA worker through GraphGoblin with Codex 0.160.0 (`workspace-write`, approval `never`, network off). Its Codex session log records the session and turn working directory as the admitted workspace `%TEMP%\gg-aidlc-trial\aidlc-trial-<timestamp>\aidlc-trial-positive`, which is what GraphGoblin passed as `--cd`. The log also records each command's own `workdir` argument, which the SDK's command items do not expose (the reason the trial could not tell these causes apart):
28	
29	| Command `workdir` named by the model                                                 | Calls | Outcome                                           |
30	| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----: | ------------------------------------------------- |
31	| `%TEMP%\gg-aidlc-trial\aidlc-trial-<timestamp>\aidlc-trial-positive` (the workspace) |     7 | all ran                                           |
32	| `%TEMP%\gg-aidlc-trial\aidlc-trial-positive` (timestamp segment dropped)             |     5 | all failed: `CreateProcessWithLogonW failed: 267` |
33	
34	The shortened directory does not exist; the trial only creates timestamped run directories, and `%TEMP%\gg-aidlc-trial` still holds only the timestamped one. The failures were therefore not intermittent in their cause: the model alternated between the correct and a mistyped path, and every mistyped call failed.
35	
36	Reproduction without a model turn, through Codex's own sandbox command (`codex sandbox -P :workspace -C <dir> -- cmd /c cd`, CLI 0.160.0):
37	
38	| Working directory                         | `elevated` (configured mode)                                          | `unelevated`                                                                |
39	| ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
40	| missing directory                         | exit 1, `windows sandbox failed: CreateProcessWithLogonW failed: 267` | exit 1, `CreateProcessAsUserW failed: 267 (The directory name is invalid.)` |
41	| existing, 258 characters                  | exit 0                                                                | exit 0                                                                      |
42	| existing, 262 characters                  | exit 1, `CreateProcessWithLogonW failed: 267`                         | exit 1, `CreateProcessAsUserW failed: 267 (The directory name is invalid.)` |
43	| every matrix directory below              | exit 0, printed the directory                                         | exit 0, printed the directory                                               |
44	| existing, `CodexSandboxUsers` denied read | exit 0                                                                | exit 0                                                                      |
45	
46	Windows error 267 is `ERROR_DIRECTORY` ("The directory name is invalid"): Windows refuses to start a process whose working directory does not exist or is longer than 258 characters. The sandbox's wrapper text differs from the trial's (`windows sandbox failed` against `Failed to create unified exec process`) because the trial went through Codex's unified exec tool; the Windows call and its error code are the same.
47

Four real occurrences appear in Codex Desktop sessions (CLI 0.162.0-alpha) that GraphGoblin did not launch; three named no per-command directory. Their causes were not analysed; they show that the message is not specific to GraphGoblin launches.

# WP-F5: Windows command-launch diagnosis

Research record for #102 (WP-F5), measured on 2026-10-19 from `main` at `9070207`. All launches used installed CLIs through their subscription logins, disposable directories, and disposable APIs on ports 5710 and 5711. No model turn was run for either provider. No credential was exported or printed: the CLIs only checked their own logins, and Claude's `auth status` output was reduced to two fields. The disposable APIs seeded the machine's Jev key from the environment into their own stores, as any instance does; those stores were deleted afterwards. The owner's instance, store and checkout were not touched. Revised on 2026-10-20 after review: the `fs.mkdtemp` boundary was re-measured at 247 characters (succeeds) and 248 (fails), and the defect classification of launch names was corrected.

## Result

**Confirmed, not a GraphGoblin launch defect.** The #102 failure (`Failed to create unified exec process: CreateProcessWithLogonW failed: 267`) is Codex's Windows sandbox refusing a command whose working directory is invalid. In the trial, the QA worker model supplied a per-command `workdir` that dropped one segment of the admitted workspace path, so the directory did not exist. GraphGoblin's `--cd` was correct, and every command that used it ran. The failure reproduces without a model turn by asking Codex's sandbox to start a command in a missing directory.

**One matrix cell failed where the direct invocation succeeded,** and it was fixed: with the system temporary directory at 226 characters, the Claude adapter's readiness check could not create its empty check directory, because Windows `fs.mkdtemp` refuses paths of 248 characters or more (the check path was 249). Claude itself starts from such a directory. The adapter now creates the directory with `mkdir`. Every other cell behaved the same through GraphGoblin as through PowerShell and `cmd`.

**Script node launches** behaved identically to direct launches in every matrix cell. The original report concerns harness launches (commands run by a Codex worker inside Codex's sandbox), not script nodes.

## Environment

| Item                     | Value                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| OS                       | Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26300, `LongPathsEnabled = 1`, console code page 65001                                                                                  |
| Node                     | 22.14.0 for every GraphGoblin launch and every `codex.js` cell; the machine default 23.10.0 ran the npm global `codex.cmd` shim and read Codex session logs |
| Codex CLI                | 0.160.0, both the SDK-bundled CLI and the npm global install; the user Codex configuration selects `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"`                         |
| Claude Code              | 2.1.304, native `claude.exe`, signed in with a Claude.ai account                                                                                            |
| Other drive              | `D:` (local NTFS)                                                                                                                                           |
| Session variables        | The Claude Code session variables of the measuring shell (`CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_CODE_*`, `CLAUDE_PID`) were removed from every launched environment         |
| Updater on Claude copies | Direct launches of copied `claude.exe` set `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1`, as the product's own Claude environment does                                            |

## The original report

The 2026-10-06 trial ran one QA worker through GraphGoblin with Codex 0.160.0 (`workspace-write`, approval `never`, network off). Its Codex session log records the session and turn working directory as the admitted workspace `%TEMP%\gg-aidlc-trial\aidlc-trial-<timestamp>\aidlc-trial-positive`, which is what GraphGoblin passed as `--cd`. The log also records each command's own `workdir` argument, which the SDK's command items do not expose (the reason the trial could not tell these causes apart):

| Command `workdir` named by the model                                                 | Calls | Outcome                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----: | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `%TEMP%\gg-aidlc-trial\aidlc-trial-<timestamp>\aidlc-trial-positive` (the workspace) |     7 | all ran                                           |
| `%TEMP%\gg-aidlc-trial\aidlc-trial-positive` (timestamp segment dropped)             |     5 | all failed: `CreateProcessWithLogonW failed: 267` |

The shortened directory does not exist; the trial only creates timestamped run directories, and `%TEMP%\gg-aidlc-trial` still holds only the timestamped one. The failures were therefore not intermittent in their cause: the model alternated between the correct and a mistyped path, and every mistyped call failed.

Reproduction without a model turn, through Codex's own sandbox command (`codex sandbox -P :workspace -C <dir> -- cmd /c cd`, CLI 0.160.0):

| Working directory                         | `elevated` (configured mode)                                          | `unelevated`                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| missing directory                         | exit 1, `windows sandbox failed: CreateProcessWithLogonW failed: 267` | exit 1, `CreateProcessAsUserW failed: 267 (The directory name is invalid.)` |
| existing, 258 characters                  | exit 0                                                                | exit 0                                                                      |
| existing, 262 characters                  | exit 1, `CreateProcessWithLogonW failed: 267`                         | exit 1, `CreateProcessAsUserW failed: 267 (The directory name is invalid.)` |
| every matrix directory below              | exit 0, printed the directory                                         | exit 0, printed the directory                                               |
| existing, `CodexSandboxUsers` denied read | exit 0                                                                | exit 0                                                                      |
